newsitem.title: LEBANON: Arab financiers say region must liberalise.
newsitem.headline: Arab financiers say region must liberalise.

text.p: Arab countries must liberalise their markets, diversify their economies and pursue reforms to meet the challenges of the next century, Arab economists and financiers told a Beirut conference on Wednesday.

Having taken encouraging steps towards economic stabilisation they must now start restructuring their economies and making full use of resources, the experts told the Third Arab Capital Markets Conference.

"Arab economies are still characterised by weakness in their production sectors and dependence on a small number of products, most of which are exported as raw material," Abdullatif al-Hamad, President of the Kuwait-based Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development, said in a speech.
Despite big investments, basic manufacturing industry had failed to become a driving force in Arab economies, Hamad told the 400 financiers and economists at the conference.
"It (manufacturing) only contributes a modest slice to the GDP of all Arab countries at 11 percent in 1996 against levels reaching 25 percent in other developing countries," he said.

Arab industry absorbed 20 percent of the labour force but industrial exports were valued at only 17 percent of the total. "This proves the existence of a structural imbalance in the formation of Arab economies," Hamad said.
Hisham Nazer, a former Saudi oil minister, said Arab countries needed to diversify their industries.

"There is an absolute importance to develop and diversify industry in the Arab world which in turn needs serious financing amid favourable investment condition," he told Reuters during the conference.
Jassem al-Mannai', President of the Arab Monetary Fund, said it was essential that Arab countries continued their attempts to reduce budget deficits and achieve higher growth levels.
"It remains a priority to achieve higher economic growth levels. We have to review our whole budget structure and restudy our labour market to deal with high unemployment rates," he told Reuters.

"Any realistic concept on the future of economic integration in the Arab world should start from an agreement to liberalise all commodities of any sort of restrictions gradually within a number of years," he added.
Mannai' said Arab economies were in a position to attract foreign capital but this required a free flow of information on their investment atmosphere and the products trading on their exchanges.
"We need to reassure foreign investors continuously of our commitment to liberal policies in order to win their confidence," he said.
Mohammed Aba al-Kheil, a former Saudi finance minister, told Reuters private financial institutions had to be created to foster investment.
"We need to develop partnerships between local financial institutions and foreign institutions in which huge capital is invested," he said.
An International Finance Corporation (IFC) report presented to the conference said Arab countries attracted $6.9 billion of the $243.8 billion in net private flows to developing countries.
It said gross private capital flows to developing countries were expected to rise substantially in the future.
